 Indonesia Parliament passes long-awaited asset forfeiture bill 
 Indonesia Parliament passes long-awaited asset forfeiture bill
 November 19, 2026 14:07 GMT+700 
 Speaker of the Indonesian House of Representatives (DPR RI) Puan Maharani (right) receives a report on the deliberation of the Asset Confiscation Bill from Chair of Commission III of the House, Habiburokhman (left), during the 13th Plenary Session of the House for the Second Sitting Period of the 2026-2027 Legislative Year at the Parliamentary Complex in Senayan, Jakarta, Thursday (Nov. 19, 2026). During the session, the House approved the Asset Confiscation Bill into law after 18 years of deliberation in the legislature. ANTARA FOTO/Fauzan/nym. (ANTARA FOTO/FAUZAN) 
 Jakarta (ANTARA) - Indonesia’s House of Representatives (DPR) on Thursday passed the long-awaited Bill on Asset Forfeiture Related to Corruption and Other Crimes into law, concluding an 18-year legislative deliberation process.
The approval took place during the 13th Plenary Session chaired by House Speaker Puan Maharani, following a final report on the bill's drafting submitted by Habiburokhman, chairman of House Commission III overseeing legal and human rights affairs.
"I will ask each faction whether the Bill on Asset Forfeiture Related to Corruption and Other Crimes can be approved and passed into law?" Puan asked the floor before striking the gavel to formalize the passage.
The plenary vote came a day after Commission III and the government concluded first-level deliberations on Wednesday, agreeing to advance the draft legislation for final approval.
According to Habiburokhman, the working committee reviewed 397 items on its problem inventory list—comprising 160 permanent clauses, 135 editorial revisions, 40 substantive amendments, 44 deletions, and 18 new substantive provisions. 
Since September 2025, the commission has also held 87 hearings to gather input from legal experts, civil society organizations, and the general public.
Outlining ten key pillars of the legislation, Habiburokhman highlighted that the law covers technology-driven fraud and embezzlement cases that inflict widespread harm on the public.
"Such as fraudulent investments and fraudulent stock trading, where the number of victims is very large and awaits justice," he said.
He noted that the legislation upholds existing criminal penalties for corruption and severe offenses, including the death penalty, in accordance with prevailing Indonesian laws.
Additionally, the law establishes a clear mandate and authority for a designated state body to professionally and accountably manage seized assets—covering their storage, security, maintenance, utilization, sale, restitution, and disposal.
